rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to maximize the chance of observing all 10 compounds while retaining early-eluting components. The retention and resolution patterns will guide subsequent adjustments to gradient range, duration, and temperature.

The scouting run has substantial resolution margin, so shorten the gradient to reduce the time penalty. Keeping composition endpoints and temperature fixed isolates the effect of gradient steepness on the closest peaks.

Increase gradient duration modestly to improve the critical separation while aiming to keep the last peak within the zero-time-penalty region. This brackets the tradeoff between the 12- and 20-minute gradients before adjusting selectivity.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to improve the critical pair while keeping the predicted last peak just under 10 minutes. All peaks have eluted well before the gradient endpoint, so lowering phi1 should not compromise recovery.

Test a modest temperature increase to adjust selectivity around the sole under-resolved pair while potentially shortening retention. Only a small resolution improvement is needed to reach the maximum score if the time penalty remains zero.

The temperature response suggests the critical pair may cross and separate again above 45 C. Test 55 C to exploit that selectivity change while retaining the zero time penalty, checking all neighboring separations for new bottlenecks.

Slightly steepen the gradient at 55 C to favor separation of the critical pair after its apparent elution-order reversal. This should also shorten the run, while the other pairs currently have resolution margin.

Shorten the gradient to 12 minutes, following the observed improvement in the critical pair with increasing gradient steepness at 55 C. This may bring its resolution above 1.5 while preserving adequate separation of the next-tightest pair and keeping the time penalty zero.

Test a slightly shallower gradient to improve the separation of peaks 4–5 while aiming to keep the other critical pair above 1.5. This nearby method may also achieve CRF 1.000 with a more balanced resolution margin and no time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test an alternative that may provide greater resolution margin. Higher temperature should further separate the previously crossed pair, while a shallower gradient may protect the other tight separation and keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Return to 55 C and test a higher starting organic fraction to change selectivity while shortening retention. This explores whether another maximum-score method can provide more clearance above R = 1.5 for both tight pairs.

Increase starting organic fraction to continue exploring the improved critical-pair selectivity, compensating with a longer gradient to protect the other close separation. The aim is another CRF 1.000 method with greater resolution margin, not a score above the established maximum.

Slightly flatten the gradient to improve the new limiting separation while retaining the resolution margin of the other close pair. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially restoring CRF 1.000 with a more balanced minimum resolution.

Further flatten the gradient slightly to balance the two closest separations, targeting a minimum resolution near 1.7. The projected last-peak time remains below 10 minutes, so this may preserve the maximum CRF while improving separation margin.

Test a nearby gradient slope with the higher final organic fraction: its slope closely matches injection 14, which had the largest minimum resolution among maximum-score methods. Expect similar separation and a last-peak time below 10 minutes, mapping another point on the CRF 1.000 plateau.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 11 to map the maximum-score region at a lower starting organic fraction. The observed trends suggest all resolutions may remain above 1.5 with the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Explore a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to seek greater critical-pair resolution while retaining CRF 1.000. Check especially the early peaks for compression and the last peak for a possible time penalty.

Return to the successful 0.10 starting fraction and test a gradient slightly steeper than injection 11. This should shorten retention while potentially balancing the two tight separations above R = 1.5 and preserving the maximum CRF.

Explore the lower-temperature selectivity branch using a gradient expected to keep the last peak below 10 minutes. Cooling should improve the pair that was limiting at 40 C, though the neighboring separation must be checked for a new bottleneck.

Return to the successful 55 C region and test a gradient slope between injections 13 and 15. This should balance the two critical separations above 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes, potentially providing another maximum-score method.

Test a slightly steeper gradient than injection 18 to shorten retention and balance its two closest separations. Both are projected to remain just above R = 1.5, potentially preserving CRF 1.000 with a shorter run.

Use the same gradient slope as injection 8 with a lower endpoint and shorter programmed gradient. Since all peaks previously eluted before this gradient would end, the separation should remain essentially unchanged and retain CRF 1.000.

Keep the successful gradient slope while lowering the endpoint to 0.65 and shortening the programmed gradient to 8 minutes. The gradient would still end at the outlet after the observed last peak, so CRF 1.000 should be preserved.

Test a shorter programmed gradient with nearly the same slope as injection 15, which achieved CRF 1.000 and minimum resolution 1.70. All peaks are expected to elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, preserving the improved separation margin.

Use the final injection to test a nearby slope bracketed by successful injections 20 and 24. This is expected to retain CRF 1.000 with both critical resolutions above 1.5 and the last peak below 10 minutes; the campaign has already reached the maximum possible score.
